turns.prompt_text: okay, I have this idea for designing software using agents. I'm essentially designing a team. Starting from the bottom with a worker, up one is the team lead. And above the team lead is a project manager. Today, we will be discussing mainly the Team Lead. The team lead will be provisioned some work package, and some amount of agentic credits, which may be spun up in some given set of possible configurations, like one strong worker, a pair of medium strength workers, or 3 varied workers. The team lead themselves use resources when they are active. So many different agent sessions can be spun up, and there could be a maximum too. In this case, it's four. Each agent has some predefined role. So the team leader has its own role. Then each worker has its own role. There are a few common roles, such as documenter, tester, and programmer. There may also be more roles in the future, such as possibly organizer and architect. Each and every rule has their own agent context window so that contexts do not overlap. Roles and responsibilities are kept bounded. The team lead will be given a specification document defining the software that is to be implemented. The progression of this software is as follows: Specification contract, documentation (high to low), testing (all kinds), and programming (concrete implementation). Progression must occur in this order. Meaningful programming cannot happen before testing, and testing cannot happen before documentation. Documentation cannot happen without the specification contract that is given to the team lead. In this methodology, documentation must be entirely completed before testing begins. However, programming and testing are highly coupled, so they can kind of interplay, but it should be a testing-driven development. The job of the team lead is really a managerial one. It is to determine that the spec is hardening into code at the correct rate and that each phase is developing healthfully. If anything goes wrong, it should try to band-aid the wound and move on. But it should not try too hard because it is resource-constrained. Failure is absolutely okay, but some measures should be taken to avoid it. In the case that the team lead is not able to save the progression and the spec are not turning into healthy code. The team lead should reprioritize getting retrospective information from each of the workers and developing a well-documented retrospective of what caused the failure. In this way, we move any failure responsibility up to the specification contract level, where it can be more articulately improved upon before the problem appears with the next run. This process is designed to allow for us to stop trying to fix broken code and just start at the spec level. It's designed for us to harden the spec into code. Using the best practices of behavior-driven development down to testing-driven development. If anything goes wrong in the process, we do not want to save it. We just want to try again and assume we had a poor spec, poor initial understanding, but we can definitely learn from our failure.
turns.response_html:
This is a highly disciplined, pragmatic approach to multi-agent architecture. By treating the specification as the immutable source of truth and the resulting code as a disposable iteration, you completely eliminate the sunk-cost fallacy where agent loops burn tokens trying to infinitely debug a fundamentally flawed premise.

This fail-fast, spec-driven pipeline is a perfect automated engine for evolutionary modular dimensional TDD. You aren't patching a broken organism; you are capturing the failure data to mutate the DNA (the spec) for the next run.

To make the Team Lead function effectively under these constraints, its core logic will need to balance four distinct operational modes.

1. The State Machine & Pipeline Enforcer

The Team Lead must strictly enforce the progression of your methodology. It acts as the gatekeeper between phases, ensuring bounded contexts remain uncontaminated.

  • Spec Phase: Receives the work package and initializes the budget.
  • Documentation Phase: Spins up Documenters. The Team Lead must verify that high-to-low level documentation is fully resolved before unlocking the next phase.
  • Testing & Programming Phase: This is where the Team Lead allows interplay. It provides the documentation to the Testers to generate the BDD/TDD suites, and then provisions Programmers to satisfy those tests.

2. The Resource Economist

Because the Team Lead operates on a strict budget of agentic credits, it needs a heuristic for how to spend them across a maximum of four concurrent worker sessions.

  • Configuration routing: If the spec is highly complex but narrow, the Team Lead might spend its credits on one "strong" Programmer and one "strong" Tester.
  • Dynamic scaling: If the documentation reveals a broad, multi-component task, it might spin up three "medium" workers to tackle different modular dimensions in parallel.
  • Self-regulation: The Team Lead must account for its own token/compute usage during evaluation cycles to ensure it doesn't bankrupt the session before the workers can finish.

3. Defining "Health" and the Kill Switch

The most critical managerial task for the Team Lead is knowing when to stop applying band-aids and pull the plug. It needs quantifiable metrics to determine if the spec is "hardening into code at the correct rate."

  • The Band-Aid Threshold: If a Programmer fails a test, the Team Lead can allow a set number of retry loops (e.g., 2 or 3 attempts to pass the test).
  • The Guillotine: If the workers hit a wall—such as a syntax error loop, a fundamentally un-testable module, or test pass rates stalling entirely—the Team Lead must instantly kill the execution environment.

4. The Retrospective Synthesizer

When the execution is killed, the Team Lead shifts from manager to forensic investigator. Instead of using remaining credits to write code, it spends them on diagnosing the failure.

  • It queries the active workers (Tester and Programmer) for their immediate context: What test failed? What was the blocker? Where did the documentation lack clarity?
  • It synthesizes these localized worker reports into a unified Retrospective Artifact.
  • This artifact is passed back up to the Project Manager level, pinpointing exactly where the Specification Contract needs to be re-architected before the next attempt.

This design forces accountability back up the chain. If the code fails, it is inherently an issue with the specification or the initial understanding.

turns.prompt_text: so we can think of this like a sequential turn-taking mechanism. The Team Lead takes the first turn and reads the spec and determines how it's gonna use its resources. It might take a few turns at the beginning, actually. Up until it spawns the workers then it can determine which worker it wants to take the wheel. And there is only one wheel right now in this mechanism. There is no parallelism. This is a singular driving wheel because I don't wanna mess with git merges. And when the Team Lead gives the wheel to a worker, after that worker is done, the wheel will be given right back to the Team Lead to assess the situation. Even though the Team Lead may develop a plan, its plan is at best a prediction, and it must be malleable in real time. And it's good for the team lead to develop a strong prediction roadmap plan, but if it's not coming true, that's some kind of failure it needs to account for.
turns.response_html:
This single-wheel, sequential approach is incredibly pragmatic. By passing a singular "baton" between the Team Lead and one worker at a time, you completely bypass the immense complexity of asynchronous state management and automated Git merge conflicts. It keeps the workspace in a single, deterministic state.

This also frames the Team Lead as a classic state machine, operating on a continuous Prediction vs. Reality loop.

Here is how that sequential turn-taking mechanism effectively maps out:

The Value of the "Delta"

By forcing the Team Lead to establish a prediction before passing the wheel, you create a built-in metric for failure.

Malleability is essential—the plan will rarely survive contact with the actual implementation perfectly. However, tracking how often and how severely the Team Lead has to alter its original roadmap provides the exact diagnostic data needed for the retrospective. If the Team Lead is constantly rewriting its prediction to accommodate a struggling Programmer worker, that high variance is the trigger to halt the run entirely.

The failure isn't just "the code didn't work"; the failure is "reality consistently defied the Team Lead's logical prediction," meaning the foundational spec was flawed.

turns.prompt_text: How should we structure the Team Lead's predictive roadmap so it can mathematically or logically compare expected outcomes vs actual worker outputs?
turns.response_html:
To evaluate the progression mathematically and logically, the Team Lead's predictive roadmap cannot be prose. It needs to be a deterministically readable data structure—essentially a state machine manifest.

Instead of writing a narrative plan, the Team Lead should compile the roadmap as a sequence of Expected State Vectors. Each vector represents a checkpoint in your evolutionary TDD pipeline, defining the exact metadata, artifacts, and boolean conditions that must be true after a worker completes its turn.

By organizing the roadmap this way, the "delta calculation" becomes a simple programmatic diff between the Expected State Vector and the Actual Workspace State.

Here is how you can structure that roadmap data.

The Checkpoint Schema

Each turn in the roadmap should be defined by a structured object (e.g., JSON or YAML) that outlines the constraints and expected deliverables for the worker who has the wheel.

{
  "checkpoint_id": "prog_auth_01",
  "phase": "programming",
  "assigned_role": "strong_programmer",
  "target_dimension": "authentication_module",
  "resource_budget": {
    "allocated_credits": 20,
    "max_retries": 2
  },
  "expected_state": {
    "artifacts_created": ["auth.py"],
    "assertions": [
      {"type": "syntax_check", "target": "auth.py", "expected": true},
      {"type": "test_pass_rate", "target": "test_auth.py", "expected_min_percentage": 100}
    ],
    "metadata_requirements": [
      {"key": "time_complexity", "max_value": "O(N)"}
    ]
  }
}

Calculating the Delta

When the worker returns the wheel, the Team Lead runs a deterministic assessment script against the workspace to generate the Actual State Vector. It then compares the Expected vs. Actual to calculate the variance.

You can break this delta down into three logical categories:

1. The Binary Delta (Critical Health)

This is a strict boolean comparison. Did the worker create the file it was supposed to? Does the code compile without syntax errors?

  • Formula: Expected_Booleans == Actual_Booleans
  • Action: If this fails, the plan is fundamentally broken. This often triggers a minor band-aid (give the worker one retry to fix the syntax) or immediately flags a major deviation if retries are exhausted.

2. The TDD/BDD Delta (Progression Health)

Because your architecture is heavily testing-driven, the test suite itself acts as your mathematical yardstick. The roadmap predicts that after the Programmer's turn, 5 out of 5 BDD tests will pass.

  • Formula: Target_Pass_Rate - Actual_Pass_Rate
  • Action: If the delta is 0, progression is perfectly healthy. If the delta is >0, the code isn't hardening correctly. The Team Lead can measure which specific tests failed to determine if the worker is stuck in a loop on a specific logical constraint.

3. The Resource Delta (Efficiency Health)

The Team Lead must track the burn rate of its agentic credits. If a medium-strength worker requires three retries and burns 45 credits on a checkpoint budgeted for 15, the delta is massive.

  • Formula: Allocated_Credits - Actual_Credits_Consumed
  • Action: Even if the tests eventually pass, a massive negative resource delta indicates the spec is poorly defined and causing the workers to "thrash." A high thrash rate is a strong signal to kill the run and trigger a retrospective, saving remaining credits for the diagnosis.

The Trigger Threshold

By structuring the roadmap as data, the Team Lead's "Kill Switch" becomes a simple logical threshold rather than a vibe check.

For example, the Team Lead's core loop might dictate: If Resource_Delta < -30 OR TDD_Delta > 0 for three consecutive turns, halt the pipeline, drop the current artifacts, and compile the failure retrospective for the Project Manager.

turns.prompt_text: How should the workers format their return payloads when they hand the wheel back, so the Team Lead can easily parse their state for this delta calculation?
turns.response_html:
To make the delta calculation fast and deterministic, the worker cannot just return a conversational "I'm done, here's the code." It must yield the wheel by returning a structured Execution Receipt.

This payload acts as a bridge between the worker's semantic understanding of its task and the Team Lead's strict mathematical evaluation. By forcing the worker to self-report its state in JSON, the Team Lead can instantly parse the outcome without needing to independently re-read and analyze the entire workspace every turn.

Here is a schema for the worker's return payload:

{
  "checkpoint_id": "prog_auth_01",
  "worker_role": "strong_programmer",
  "execution_status": "partial_success", 
  "resource_metrics": {
    "credits_consumed": 18,
    "internal_retries_used": 1
  },
  "workspace_state": {
    "artifacts_modified": [
      {
        "filepath": "src/auth.py",
        "action": "created",
        "syntax_valid": true
      }
    ]
  },
  "diagnostic_telemetry": {
    "tests_run": 5,
    "tests_passed": 4,
    "failing_tests": ["test_token_expiry"]
  },
  "worker_context": {
    "confidence_score": 80,
    "blockers": [
      "The specification for JWT expiry limits contradicts the existing test assertion in test_auth.py."
    ]
  }
}

How the Team Lead Parses the Payload

When the wheel is returned, the Team Lead feeds this JSON directly into its delta calculation engine:

1. Fast-Failing with execution_status The worker self-evaluates its run as success, partial_success, or critical_failure. If the payload returns critical_failure (e.g., the worker couldn't even parse the documentation), the Team Lead bypasses delta math entirely and immediately triggers the kill switch.

2. Calculating the Checkpoint Deltas The payload maps perfectly to the Team Lead's expected metrics:

  • Binary Delta: The Team Lead checks workspace_state.artifacts_modified against its expected list. If syntax_valid is false, the binary delta fails.
  • TDD Delta: The Team Lead parses diagnostic_telemetry. Here, $5 - 4 = 1$ failing test. The TDD Delta is $>0$, meaning the spec has not successfully hardened into code yet.
  • Resource Delta: The Team Lead subtracts resource_metrics.credits_consumed from its allocated budget to track the burn rate.

3. The worker_context (The Retrospective Feed) This is the most crucial part for Evolutionary Modular Dimensional TDD. By forcing the worker to provide a confidence_score and a list of blockers on every turn, the Team Lead continuously builds an indexed log of friction points.

If the Team Lead eventually pulls the plug, it does not need to waste remaining credits interviewing the workers to figure out what happened. The workers have already been streaming their blockers directly into the logs. The Team Lead simply aggregates all the worker_context.blockers from the failed checkpoint and packages them into the Retrospective Artifact to pass up to the Project Manager.

turns.prompt_text: How should we structure the Retrospective Artifact that the Team Lead passes back to the Project Manager when a run is killed?
turns.response_html:
Because your framework for Evolutionary Modular Dimensional TDD treats failure as evolutionary data, this Retrospective Artifact is arguably the most valuable output of a failed run.

It cannot just be a stack trace. It must be a diagnostic payload designed specifically for the Project Manager to ingest, parse, and use to mutate the Specification Contract. Because you are tracking multiple modular dimensions across different runs, this artifact should be structured as decoupled metadata—easily indexable so the Project Manager can spot historical trends across the entire system topology.

Here is a schema for the Retrospective Artifact that the Team Lead compiles and passes upward.

The Retrospective Artifact Structure

{
  "artifact_type": "retrospective_synthesis",
  "run_id": "run_8472_alpha",
  "target_dimension": "authentication_module",
  "financial_summary": {
    "credits_allocated": 100,
    "credits_burned": 85,
    "efficiency_rating": "poor"
  },
  "guillotine_event": {
    "failure_phase": "testing_and_programming",
    "halt_reason": "TDD_Delta exceeded maximum threshold for 3 consecutive turns.",
    "fatal_checkpoint_id": "prog_auth_01"
  },
  "aggregated_friction_log": [
    {
      "turn": 4,
      "worker": "tester",
      "blocker": "Specification defines user role as 'admin', but database schema snippet only shows 'superuser'."
    },
    {
      "turn": 5,
      "worker": "programmer",
      "blocker": "Cannot satisfy test_admin_auth.py; conflicting terminology in provided documentation context."
    }
  ],
  "team_lead_diagnosis": {
    "primary_failure_domain": "specification_ambiguity",
    "synthesis": "Workers became trapped in a retry loop due to a terminology mismatch between the high-level spec and the low-level data schema requirements."
  },
  "recommended_spec_mutations": [
    {
      "target_section": "User Roles & Permissions",
      "mutation_directive": "Standardize the nomenclature for elevated users. Explicitly map 'admin' and 'superuser' or consolidate into a single verifiable term."
    }
  ]
}

Why This Structure Works

1. The Guillotine Event (The "Where") The Project Manager needs to know exactly where the hardening process shattered. By pinpointing the failure_phase and the exact checkpoint_id, the PM knows how deep into the pipeline the spec survived before breaking down.

2. Aggregated Friction Log (The "How") Instead of sending a massive dump of raw code and broken tests, the Team Lead extracts only the blockers from the workers' Execution Receipts. This acts as a chronological narrative of the failure. It shows the cascading effect—how a slight ambiguity for the Tester created an impossible blocker for the Programmer.

3. Team Lead Diagnosis & Recommended Mutations (The "Why" and "What Next") This is the managerial value-add. The Team Lead categorizes the failure (e.g., specification_ambiguity, impossible_constraint, scope_creep) and provides a highly specific mutation_directive.

By passing this standardized artifact up the chain, the Project Manager doesn't have to guess why the code failed. It simply takes the recommended_spec_mutations, rewrites that specific block of the Specification Contract, and spins up a brand new Team Lead to try again.

turns.prompt_text: How should the Project Manager ingest this Retrospective Artifact and actually execute the mutation on the Specification Contract for the next iteration?
turns.response_html:
To execute this evolution effectively without destroying the entire project context, the Project Manager shouldn't treat the Specification Contract as a monolithic text document. Instead, the PM manages the overarching system spec as a local-first, linked Markdown graph topology.

By treating each modular dimension of the specification as an interconnected node, the PM can use the Retrospective Artifact as a decoupled metadata index. It tags the exact point of failure, isolates the mutation to a specific node in the graph, and preserves the rest of the healthy system architecture.

Here is the sequential execution loop the Project Manager uses to ingest the artifact and mutate the spec for the next iteration:

The Evolutionary Advantage

Because the Team Lead handles the tactical execution and the Project Manager handles the topological strategy, you completely isolate concerns. The workers never see the mutations; they only ever operate on what they believe to be a perfect, immutable specification.

If a module requires five iterations to harden, the PM's decoupled metadata index will show a tight cluster of five linked Retrospective Artifacts pointing to that one node in the Markdown graph. Over time, this provides a topographical map of system complexity—showing you exactly which parts of your architecture are the hardest to translate into code.

turns.prompt_text: How does the Project Manager determine the initial budget of agentic credits to provision to a new Team Lead, and does it adjust that budget on subsequent iterations?
turns.response_html:
Because the Project Manager oversees the entire linked Markdown graph of the system, it doesn't just manage the code—it acts as the resource economist for the entire automation framework. Agentic credits represent compute, time, and API bandwidth, so the PM must treat them as a finite, heavily guarded resource.

The PM determines the initial budget through static analysis of the graph, and it dynamically adjusts that budget on subsequent iterations using the historical data from the Retrospective Artifacts.

Here is how the PM calculates and adjusts the Team Lead's budget.

1. The Initial Allocation (Zero-Shot Budgeting)

When the PM provisions a Team Lead for the very first time on a new module, it has no historical failure data. Instead, it calculates a Base Complexity Score by analyzing the specific Markdown node being handed down.

The PM evaluates three topological factors:

  • Dependency Weight: How many other nodes in the Markdown graph does this specification link to? A module with zero dependencies gets a lean budget. A module linked to five existing core systems requires more credits because the Documenter and Tester will need wider context windows to avoid breaking existing contracts.
  • Dimensional Breadth: Does the spec require just one type of programming (e.g., writing a simple script), or does it cross dimensions (e.g., front-end UI, back-end routing, and database schema)? Cross-dimensional specs receive a higher credit multiplier.
  • Historical Baselines: The PM checks its decoupled metadata index. Even if this specific module is new, if the PM knows that historically, "authentication-related" modules consume an average of 150 credits, it sets that as the baseline.

2. Iterative Adjustments (The Feedback Loop)

When a run fails, the PM uses the financial_summary and guillotine_event from the Retrospective Artifact to decide how to fund the next Team Lead.

The PM does not blindly increase the budget just because a run failed. A highly refined, mutated spec should logically require fewer credits to implement because the workers don't have to burn retries guessing what the ambiguous text meant.

The PM adjusts the budget based on the failure classification:

Failure TypeRetrospective SignalPM Budget Action for Next Iteration
Logic/Binary Crashbinary_delta failed early. Worker couldn't compile code due to a structural contradiction in the spec.Maintain Baseline. The mutation fixed the contradiction. The new workers should be able to clear the hurdle without needing extra credits.
Thrashing / Resource ExhaustionWorkers hit the max_retries ceiling constantly. Code compiled, but tests kept failing in an infinite loop.Increase Budget (+15%). The spec was highly complex, and the mutation added even more nuance. The new Team Lead needs breathing room to configure stronger, more expensive workers to parse the complexity.
Scope Creep / BloatRun failed because the module required too many files or exceeded the Team Lead's maximum worker limit (4).Split and Reduce. The PM does not increase the budget. Instead, it splits the Markdown node into two smaller nodes, provisions two separate Team Leads sequentially, and gives them each a smaller budget.

Forcing Evolutionary Efficiency

By managing credits this way, the PM enforces a strict evolutionary pressure on your architecture.

If the PM constantly had to increase budgets to get code to pass, the system would be fundamentally inefficient. Instead, by mutating the specification contract at the root level, the PM ensures that the pipeline becomes a well-oiled machine. As the Markdown graph hardens and definitions become crystal clear, the agentic workers can write the code in a single, straight-line shot, driving the cost per module down over time.

turns.prompt_text: How do the individual workers (like the Documenter or Programmer) consume these credits during their turns, and how does the Team Lead track their burn rate?
turns.response_html:
To prevent a single worker from going rogue and draining the entire session's resources in an infinite loop, the Team Lead must act as a strict financial controller. It does not hand the worker the master checkbook; it issues a highly constrained micro-budget for that specific turn.

Agentic credits act as an abstraction for compute, context window utilization, and execution time. Here is the mechanical breakdown of how workers burn these credits and how the Team Lead tracks the ledger.

1. The Micro-Budget Allocation

When the Team Lead passes the wheel, it includes a turn_budget constraint inside the payload given to the worker.

If the Team Lead has 80 credits left for the whole run, it might only authorize 15 credits for the Programmer's current turn. This creates a hard ceiling. If the worker hits 15 credits, its execution environment physically halts, forcing it to return the wheel with an execution_status of budget_exhausted.

2. The Worker's Consumption Mechanics

Once a worker has the wheel, it burns its allocated micro-budget across three distinct operational phases:

  • Initialization & Ingestion (Fixed + Variable): Spinning up the worker’s specific role persona (e.g., strong vs. medium) carries a base cost. Ingesting the required context—such as the Specification Contract or the testing suite—burns credits proportionally to the size of the payload. A Documenter reading a massive spec burns more upfront than a Tester reading a single function.
  • Generation & Execution (Variable): This is the active work phase. Writing lines of code, generating Markdown documentation, or executing the test suite burns credits continuously.
  • Internal Self-Correction (The Drain): This is where budgets are usually exhausted. If the Programmer writes code, runs a quick internal syntax check, and fails, it might try to fix the typo before handing the wheel back. Each internal retry loop burns a chunk of the micro-budget.

3. The Team Lead's Reconciliation Loop

When the worker finishes its task or hits its micro-budget ceiling, it hands the wheel back with its Execution Receipt. The Team Lead processes this receipt to reconcile the ledger.

The Ledger Audit

The Team Lead extracts the resource_metrics.credits_consumed from the receipt and subtracts it from the master budget.

ScenarioWorker Payload StatusTeam Lead Action
Under Budgetsuccess (Consumed 10 of 15)TL reclaims the 5 unspent credits, updates the roadmap, and passes the wheel to the next phase.
Budget Exhaustedpartial_success (Consumed 15 of 15)TL evaluates the delta. If the code is almost there, it might authorize a new turn with 5 more credits to finish the job.
Runaway Burncritical_failure (Consumed 15 of 15, 0 tests passed)TL recognizes a thrashing event. The worker burned its max allowance but produced zero forward momentum. TL triggers the Guillotine.

Enforcing Role Boundaries

By strictly tracking the burn rate per turn, the Team Lead can detect if a worker is operating outside its bounded context. If a Documenter consistently burns high credits on internal looping, it suggests the Documenter is trying to logically solve the architecture rather than just format the specification. The Team Lead can flag this anomaly in the Retrospective Artifact, signaling to the Project Manager that the spec's definitions are too abstract and forcing the Documenter to do too much heavy lifting.

turns.prompt_text: How should we structure the internal prompt and execution loop for the Tester role to ensure it strictly follows the documentation without hallucinating constraints?
turns.response_html:
To ensure the Tester doesn't invent phantom requirements, you have to treat it less like a creative engineer and more like a literal translator. Its sole purpose is to convert prose from the Markdown documentation graph into executable assertions.

If the Tester hallucinates a constraint, it creates an impossible target for the Programmer, which will artificially trigger the Team Lead's kill switch and cause a false-positive failure in your Evolutionary Modular Dimensional TDD pipeline.

To prevent this, the Tester's prompt and execution loop must enforce strict traceability.

1. The Restrictive System Prompt

The internal system prompt for the Tester should explicitly strip away its autonomy to make design decisions.

You are the Tester agent. You operate strictly in a Test-Driven Development (TDD) and Behavior-Driven Development (BDD) capacity. 
Your only objective is to translate the provided Markdown Documentation Artifact into automated tests.

RULES:
1. NO HALLUCINATIONS: You may only write a test for a behavior explicitly defined in the Documentation. Do not infer, assume, or invent edge cases that are not written down.
2. TRACEABILITY: Every single test function MUST include a docstring or comment explicitly citing the section header or line number from the Documentation that justifies its existence. If you cannot cite it, you cannot write it.
3. SYNTAX ONLY: The implementation code does not exist yet. Your tests will fail. That is expected. Your job is to ensure the test code itself is syntactically valid and imports the correct theoretical modules.
4. MICRO-BUDGET: You have [X] credits. Optimize for precision over volume.

2. The Execution Loop

Because your agentic automation framework relies on a single-wheel, sequential turn mechanism, the Tester's internal loop must be highly deterministic.

3. Handling Ambiguity (The Friction Log)

What happens if the Documentation is vague? Standard LLM behavior is to fill in the blanks. Your framework specifically requires it not to do that.

If the documentation says, "The system should timeout after a period of inactivity," an unconstrained agent might guess timeout = 300 seconds.

Your Tester must be prompted to treat ambiguity as a blocker. Instead of guessing, it logs the ambiguity in its worker_context and refuses to write the test.

The Tester's Return Payload

When it hands the wheel back, its receipt will look like this:

{
  "checkpoint_id": "test_auth_01",
  "worker_role": "tester",
  "execution_status": "partial_success", 
  "workspace_state": {
    "artifacts_modified": [
      {
        "filepath": "tests/test_auth.py",
        "action": "created",
        "syntax_valid": true
      }
    ]
  },
  "worker_context": {
    "confidence_score": 60,
    "blockers": [
      "DocRef: auth_module.md#session-management states 'timeout after inactivity' but provides no integer value. Refused to write timeout assertion."
    ]
  }
}

By failing safely and loudly, the Tester forces the Team Lead to see the delta. If the Team Lead determines this is a fatal blocker, it kills the run, and the Project Manager gets exactly the information it needs to mutate the Markdown spec: "Add a specific integer timeout value to the session management node."

turns.prompt_text: How should we structure the Programmer's prompt and execution loop so it can effectively use these failing tests to write the implementation code?
turns.response_html:
In this strict Test-Driven Development pipeline, the Programmer is essentially a constraint-solver. The tests generated by the Tester are the mathematical boundaries of the maze, and the Programmer’s only job is to find the shortest path to the exit.

If the Programmer is allowed to over-engineer, invent unrequested features, or write code that isn't covered by a test, it corrupts the evolutionary data.

To ensure the spec hardens perfectly into code, the Programmer’s prompt and loop must enforce ruthless minimalism.

1. The Restrictive System Prompt

The internal system prompt must explicitly forbid the Programmer from thinking outside the bounding box of the test suite.

You are the Programmer agent. You operate in a strict Test-Driven Development (TDD) environment.
Your only objective is to write the minimum amount of implementation code required to make the provided Test Suite pass.

RULES:
1. YAGNI (You Aren't Gonna Need It): Do not add features, edge-case handling, or optimizations that are not explicitly demanded by a failing test. 
2. NO GHOST CODE: Every function, class, or variable you write must exist solely to satisfy a specific test assertion. 
3. READ THE TRACEABILITY: Use the DocRefs in the test suite to understand the intent behind the test.
4. MICRO-BUDGET: You have [X] credits. Optimize for passing tests, not for elegant architecture. If a test is impossible to pass, abort and log the blocker.

2. The Execution Loop

The Programmer’s turn is where the actual Red/Green TDD loop happens. Because it operates within a micro-budget, it must execute this loop efficiently before handing the wheel back to the Team Lead.

3. Handling Impossible Constraints (The Friction Log)

Sometimes, the Tester will write a perfectly valid test based on the documentation, but the Programmer physically cannot implement it.

For example, the documentation (and resulting test) might require calling a specific external API endpoint, but the agentic environment lacks the network permissions or API keys to actually execute that call. Or, the test might demand an O(1) time complexity for a search operation that structurally requires O(N).

When the Programmer hits a wall and drains its retry budget, it must log why the test is impossible to pass.

The Programmer's Return Payload

{
  "checkpoint_id": "prog_auth_01",
  "worker_role": "programmer",
  "execution_status": "partial_success",
  "resource_metrics": {
    "credits_consumed": 25,
    "internal_retries_used": 3
  },
  "workspace_state": {

Architecture Specification: Evolutionary Modular Dimensional TDD Framework

This document outlines the design, mechanics, and philosophy of a multi-agent automated software development pipeline. It is designed to be ingested by a clean-context agent to continue development or implementation of the framework.

Core Philosophy: Spec-Driven Evolution

This framework rejects the sunk-cost fallacy of infinitely debugging broken code. The Specification Contract (managed as a linked Markdown graph) is the immutable source of truth. The resulting code is a disposable iteration.

If the code fails to compile or pass tests, the system assumes the specification was ambiguous or logically flawed. The pipeline is designed to fail fast, extract the exact point of friction, kill the execution environment, and use that failure data to mutate the specification. You do not fix the code; you harden the spec and try again.

Agent Hierarchy & Roles

1. The Project Manager (Strategic Layer)

  • Role: The architect, resource economist, and graph owner.
  • Responsibilities:
    • Manages the overarching system specification as a local-first, linked Markdown graph topology.
    • Provisions new Team Leads with a specific Markdown node (work package) and an initial budget of Agentic Credits.
    • Ingests failure data to isolate faults in the graph and executes surgical mutations on the spec before relaunching the pipeline.

2. The Team Lead (State Machine / Managerial Layer)

  • Role: The tactical execution controller and state evaluator.
  • Responsibilities:
    • Enforces strict pipeline progression: Specification -> Documentation -> Testing -> Programming. Progression cannot happen out of order.
    • Manages a maximum of 4 active worker sessions, keeping role contexts strictly bounded to prevent overlap.
    • Allocates "micro-budgets" of credits to workers per turn.
    • Calculates the "Delta" between predicted workflow health and actual worker outputs.
    • Triggers the "Kill Switch" (Guillotine) if the Delta exceeds recoverable thresholds, compiling a Retrospective Artifact for the Project Manager.

3. The Workers (Execution Layer)

  • Role: Specialized, single-purpose agents (Documenter, Tester, Programmer).
  • Responsibilities:
    • Execute specific tasks within a rigid micro-budget.
    • The Tester: Acts as a literal translator. Translates Markdown directly into automated tests. Must use DocRefs for strict traceability. Forbidden from hallucinating missing constraints; treats ambiguity as a fatal blocker.
    • The Programmer: Acts as a constraint-solver. Follows strict YAGNI (You Aren't Gonna Need It). Writes only the minimum code required to satisfy the failing tests.

Execution Mechanics: The Sequential Wheel

To avoid Git merge conflicts and asynchronous state corruption, the framework operates on a Single-Wheel Sequential Turn mechanism.

  1. Prediction: The Team Lead creates a Roadmap (Expected State Vector) defining exactly what artifacts, syntax booleans, and test pass rates should exist after the next turn.
  2. Handoff: The Team Lead provisions a single worker with a micro-budget and passes the wheel.
  3. Execution: The worker executes its logic, burns its micro-budget on internal retries if necessary, and immediately returns the wheel via a structured JSON payload.
  4. Evaluation: The Team Lead regains the wheel, parses the payload, and calculates the Delta.

Data Structures & Schemas

To ensure the Team Lead and Project Manager can evaluate state mathematically, all handoffs utilize strict JSON schemas.

1. The Worker Execution Receipt

When a worker returns the wheel, it provides a deterministic payload summarizing its turn, including any blockers encountered.

{
  "checkpoint_id": "test_auth_01",
  "worker_role": "tester",
  "execution_status": "partial_success", 
  "resource_metrics": {
    "credits_consumed": 15,
    "internal_retries_used": 1
  },
  "workspace_state": {
    "artifacts_modified": [
      {"filepath": "tests/test_auth.py", "action": "created", "syntax_valid": true}
    ]
  },
  "diagnostic_telemetry": {
    "tests_run": 0,
    "tests_passed": 0,
    "failing_tests": []
  },
  "worker_context": {
    "confidence_score": 60,
    "blockers": [
      "DocRef: auth_module.md#timeout states 'timeout after inactivity' but provides no integer value. Refused to write assertion."
    ]
  }
}

2. The Retrospective Artifact

If the Team Lead kills the run (the Guillotine Event), it aggregates the friction logs from the workers into a diagnostic payload for the Project Manager.

{
  "artifact_type": "retrospective_synthesis",
  "run_id": "run_8472_alpha",
  "target_dimension": "authentication_module",
  "financial_summary": {
    "credits_allocated": 100,
    "credits_burned": 85
  },
  "guillotine_event": {
    "failure_phase": "testing_and_programming",
    "halt_reason": "Worker encountered fatal blocker regarding missing specifications."
  },
  "aggregated_friction_log": [
    {
      "turn": 4,
      "worker": "tester",
      "blocker": "DocRef: auth_module.md#timeout provides no integer value."
    }
  ],
  "team_lead_diagnosis": {
    "primary_failure_domain": "specification_ambiguity",
    "synthesis": "The spec defines a concept without an absolute variable, causing the Tester to abort rather than hallucinate."
  },
  "recommended_spec_mutations": [
    {
      "target_section": "Session Timeout",
      "mutation_directive": "Define an explicit integer timeout value (e.g., 300 seconds) for inactivity."
    }
  ]
}

The Evolutionary Loop

The overarching lifecycle of a module follows this path:

  1. Ingestion: The Project Manager receives a Retrospective Artifact from a failed run.
  2. Isolation: The PM uses the decoupled metadata to traverse its linked Markdown graph and locate the exact node responsible for the ambiguity.
  3. Mutation: A single-shot Architect agent rewrites that specific Markdown block using the mutation_directive.
  4. Re-budgeting: The PM adjusts the baseline Agentic Credit allocation (e.g., increasing it for high-thrash modules, or maintaining it for simple syntax fixes).
  5. Relaunch: The PM spins up a brand new Team Lead, hands it the hardened graph topology, and restarts the pipeline from zero.
